metadata.title: PISA 2009 Results: Students On Line: Digital Technologies and Performance (Volume VI)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report is based on PISA 2009, which uses a complex two-stage sampling design (schools and students within schools) to produce population-representative estimates for each participating country/economy. The text indicates that OECD uses weighted procedures for reporting school-level information (principals’ responses are weighted to be proportional to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school), implying the broader use of survey weights in estimation. However, the excerpt does not name specific student weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so the exact weighting implementation cannot be verified from the provided text. For analysts using the PISA database, the standard practice is to apply the provided student sampling weights and replicate weights when estimating standard errors and confidence intervals; the report’s focus is descriptive and model-based at the country and student levels rather than ML model training.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The excerpt does not describe how missing questionnaire or background data were handled (e.g., complete-case deletion vs. multiple imputation), which is a reporting gap for methodological transparency. While PISA cognitive outcomes are typically based on plausible values, the provided text does not specify the missing-data strategy used for the contextual variables included in the models. Given that the report presents many regression-based associations and variance-explained results, the missing-data approach materially affects reproducibility and should be documented in the full technical documentation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report describes PISA 2009 overall and then focuses on subsets for specific optional components: (i) a digital reading assessment administered in 19 countries/economies (16 OECD plus 3 partner economies), and (ii) an ICT familiarity questionnaire administered in 45 countries/economies (29 OECD plus 16 partner countries/economies). For the digital reading analyses, the report uses the student sample that participated in the digital reading option; for ICT familiarity analyses, it uses the subset that administered the optional ICT familiarity component. Where analyses compare across both print and digital reading, the report restricts to the 16 OECD countries that participated in both modes. The excerpt does not provide per-analysis inclusion/exclusion rules beyond these component-based restrictions.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report synthesizes results from PISA 2009, including a digital reading assessment administered to 15-year-olds in 19 countries/economies and an optional ICT familiarity questionnaire in 45 countries/economies. The report describes how students’ navigation behaviors in constrained digital tasks relate to digital reading performance, and how background, engagement, reading strategies, and ICT access/use are associated with digital reading proficiency. It also presents multilevel regression models (student and school levels) to quantify associations and explained variance, including the role of print reading proficiency as a covariate. The report reports descriptive benchmarks such as proportions visiting relevant pages, mean digital reading scale scores for navigation patterns, and variance explained by indices (e.g., enjoyment of reading explaining about 14% of digital reading variation on average). Methodologically, the excerpt does not specify missing-data handling for contextual variables, and it does not provide explicit ML model training details because the analyses are not framed as predictive ML pipelines.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD PISA technical results volume rather than an empirical ML paper. The excerpt provides extensive descriptive and regression-based associations and policy implications, but it does not specify any machine-learning algorithm training/evaluation pipeline, nor does it report ML-specific performance metrics. Therefore, ML technique fields are left empty and no StructuredFinding rows are fabricated.
